chief_complaint: episodic pounding headaches, sweating, and rapid heartbeat
hpi_details: 48M reporting sudden severe episodes of throbbing headache, drenching diaphoresis, and BP spikes up to 200/110. High plasma metanephrines.
ideas: He thinks he is having intense panic attacks or that his current blood pressure medication has abruptly stopped working.
concerns: He is worried he will have a sudden blood pressure surge while driving on the highway and suffer a fatal car crash or stroke.
expectations: He hopes to get a stronger medication to keep his blood pressure from spiking dangerously and a referral to a heart specialist.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pheochromocytoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes biochemical confirmation with plasma or urinary metanephrines followed by adrenal imaging and preoperative alpha-blockade, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: episodic pounding headaches, sweating, and rapid heartbeat
Key HPI features: 48M reporting sudden severe episodes of throbbing headache, drenching diaphoresis, and BP spikes up to 200/110. High plasma metanephrines.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals (between episodes): HR 82, BP 148/90; during episodes BP spikes to 200/110. Physical exam normal between attacks. Lab screening: Plasma free metanephrines markedly elevated; 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines elevated.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pheochromocytoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Panic disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe blood pressure spikes.
management_principles: Order CT or MRI of abdomen/adrenals with adrenal protocol after biochemical confirmation

Initiate mandatory preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade with Phenoxybenzamine (or Doxazosin) for 10-14 days BEFORE initiating any beta-blocker (to prevent hypertensive crisis), then surgical consultation for adrenalectomy
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Identify the classic symptom triad of pheochromocytoma (headache, sweating, tachycardia)
Select appropriate biochemical screening tests (plasma free or 24-hour urinary metanephrines)
Explain the absolute critical rule of alpha-blockade before beta-blockade in pheochromocytoma

teaching.one_liner: A catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumor causing episodic headache, sweating, and severe blood pressure spikes, confirmed by elevated plasma metanephrines.

must_ask.say: What happens during an episode — headache, sweating, racing heart?
How often do these episodes happen?
How high does your blood pressure go?
Any family history of similar episodes?

history.answer: I've been having sudden, terrible pounding headaches along with heavy sweating and a racing heart.
The headache hits all of a sudden, reaching its peak intensity within just one to two minutes.
These episodes started about a month ago, and they happen around two or three times each week.
Each attack lasts about fifteen to thirty minutes before it fades away. They can happen at any time of day or night.
The pain is all over my head, but it pounds hardest at both temples and the back of my head.
It's an intense throbbing and pounding, like my pulse is hammering inside my skull. I would rate it an eight or nine out of ten.
I checked my home blood pressure monitor during an attack last week, and it spiked to 200 over 110.
Every attack has the exact same pattern: a severe pounding headache, drenching sweat, and my heart racing fast.
Sometimes bending over, emotional stress, or strenuous effort seems to trigger it, but other times it starts out of nowhere.
Nothing makes it better while it's happening, so I just sit still and wait. Moving around or straining makes the pounding worse.
Yes, my heart pounds violently in my chest and I break out in drenching sweats that soak my shirt.
I get a sudden surge of intense panic and jitteriness during the spells, but it goes away completely once the attack ends.
No, I don't get flashing lights, zigzag lines, blind spots, or tingling before the headache starts.
I feel mildly nauseated during the worst pain, but I haven't vomited. Bright lights and loud sounds don't bother me.
No, my eyes don't get red or watery, and my nose doesn't get congested or runny.
No, I haven't had any fever, my neck isn't stiff, and I have no skin rash.
No, I haven't had any weakness, numbness, facial drooping, slurred speech, or seizures.
No, my vision has stayed completely normal with no blurriness or double vision, and my eyes don't hurt.
No, my temples are not tender to touch, and my jaw doesn't ache when I chew.
No, I haven't had any head injuries or falls recently.
I tried taking acetaminophen and ibuprofen a few times, but they didn't help the pain at all.
No, my family is completely fine, and we don't have any unvented gas heaters or carbon monoxide alarms going off.
No, I have never had cancer and I don't have any immune system conditions.
I've lost about five pounds over the past month without dieting, and I seem to get hot and sweaty much more easily.
I thought maybe I've started having massive panic attacks out of nowhere, or that my blood pressure pills completely stopped working.
I'm terrified that one of these huge surges will hit while I'm driving on the highway and cause a sudden stroke or crash.
I'm hoping to get a stronger medicine to stop these dangerous spikes immediately, and maybe a referral to a heart specialist.
I have a history of high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, both diagnosed about three years ago.
I have never had any surgeries, and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once daily for my blood pressure. I don't take any supplements or over-the-counter drugs regularly.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or nicotine products.
I only drink socially, having maybe one or two beers on the weekend.
I work full-time as an accountant, and I live at home with my wife and our two teenage children.
My father had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of adrenal tumors, endocrine conditions, or early strokes.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 148/90 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C.
Well-nourished man sitting comfortably, alert, oriented, and currently not in acute distress or diaphoretic.
Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light; extraocular movements intact; fundoscopic examination shows sharp disc margins without papilledema or hemorrhages.
No tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses; temporal arteries are pulsatile, soft, and non-tender bilaterally.
Supple neck with full active and passive range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial movements and intact facial sensation.
Normal muscle bulk and tone; 5/5 motor strength throughout all four extremities bilaterally.
Sensation to light touch and pinprick is intact and symmetric across all dermatomes.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements intact; gait is steady with normal tandem walk.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Clear to auscultation bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds and no wheezes or crackles.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender; no palpable masses or hepatosplenomegaly.
No resting or postural tremor visible in the outstretched hands.
